title: “GOD TOLD ME.” BUT DID HE? — THE TERRIFYING REALITY BEHIND “TEST EVERY SPIRIT”
paragraphs: “GOD TOLD ME.” BUT DID HE? — THE TERRIFYING REALITY BEHIND “TEST EVERY SPIRIT”

Not every voice that mentions God came from God. Not every spiritual feeling is the Holy Spirit. Not every preacher holding a Bible is faithfully speaking for Christ. And one of the most dangerous places a Christian can live is where everything supernatural is believed simply because it feels spiritual.
“God told me.”
Four words.

Four words powerful enough to change a marriage, redirect a ministry, empty a bank account, end a friendship, justify a relationship, follow a preacher, abandon a church, make a reckless decision—or silence every person who dares to ask questions.
“God told me.”
And sometimes...
God really has spoken through His Word and providentially directed His child.
But sometimes He did not.
That is precisely why Scripture gives us a command many Christians quote but far fewer seem prepared to obey:
Test it.
The apostle John wrote:
Ἀγαπητοί, μὴ παντὶ πνεύματι πιστεύετε, ἀλλὰ δοκιμάζετε τὰ πνεύματα εἰ ἐκ τοῦ θεοῦ ἐστιν
Agapētoi, mē panti pneumati pisteuete, alla dokimazete ta pneumata ei ek tou theou estin.
In straightforward English:
“Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God.”
Then John tells us why:
“because many false prophets have gone out into the world.”
—1 John 4:1
Read that slowly.
John did not write, “Beloved, believe everything supernatural.”
He did not write, “If someone says Jesus, trust him.”
He did not write, “If it gives you goosebumps, God must be in it.”
He did not write, “If the preacher has millions of followers, do not question him.”
He did not write, “If someone says, ‘The Lord told me,’ turn off your discernment.”
He said:
δοκιμάζετε — dokimazete.
Test.
Examine.
Put the claim under scrutiny.
And here is what makes the verse even more sobering: John connects the language of “spirits” immediately with false prophets who have entered the world.
The danger is not merely something mysterious whispering in a dark room.
The danger can have a microphone.
A platform.
A Bible.
Christian vocabulary.
A beautiful testimony.
A convincing personality.
A viral video.
A prophetic-sounding declaration.
And sometimes the most dangerous deception is not the thing that looks completely evil.
It is the thing that looks almost Christian.
Almost biblical.
Almost true.
Because nobody needs discernment to recognize a message saying, “Reject Jesus and worship Satan.”
The frightening deception is the message that mentions Jesus while quietly changing who Jesus is.
The message that quotes Scripture while twisting what Scripture means.
The message that promises blessing while removing repentance.
The message that talks constantly about destiny but rarely about holiness.
The message that offers crowns without crosses, breakthrough without obedience, forgiveness without repentance, Christianity without Christ as Lord.
That is where discernment becomes costly.
Because biblical discernment sometimes requires you to question something you desperately wanted to believe.
And perhaps that is where this becomes personal.
Maybe you have prayed desperately for an answer.
Maybe someone approached you and said, “God showed me something about you.”
Your heart jumped.
Finally.
Direction.
Confirmation.
An answer.
Maybe what they said sounded exactly like what you hoped God would say.
And because you wanted it to be true...
you never tested it.
That is one of the vulnerabilities of the human heart.
We often scrutinize words we dislike while eagerly accepting words that confirm what we already desire.
But Scripture does not say:
“Test only the spirits you disagree with.”
It says:
“Test the spirits.”
Even the comforting ones.
Even the exciting ones.
Even the ones spoken by people you admire.
Even mine.
Yes.
Even this article.
Do not believe something merely because Gospel Warrior published it.
Open your Bible.
Read the passage.
Look at its context.
Ask whether what you are reading faithfully represents what God has actually revealed.
Because biblical ministry should never be afraid of an open Bible.
Truth does not need you to switch off your mind.
Jesus said the greatest commandment includes loving God with all your mind.
The Bereans were commended because they received apostolic preaching eagerly while examining the Scriptures daily to determine whether what they were hearing was true.
Think about that.
They listened.
Then they checked.
That is not rebellion.
That is wisdom.
And this is where 1 John becomes even more Christ-centered.
John does not leave “testing the spirits” as some vague mystical exercise where Christians attempt to identify invisible entities through feelings.
He immediately brings the test toward Jesus Christ:
πᾶν πνεῦμα ὃ ὁμολογεῖ Ἰησοῦν Χριστὸν ἐν σαρκὶ ἐληλυθότα ἐκ τοῦ θεοῦ ἐστιν
“Every spirit that confesses Jesus Christ having come in the flesh is from God.”
—1 John 4:2
There it is.
Jesus Christ.
Not your intuition at the center.
Not the prophet at the center.
Not the experience at the center.
Not manifestations at the center.
Christ.
John's immediate concern includes the true confession of Jesus Christ coming in the flesh.
Christian discernment therefore cannot be reduced to asking, “Did this make me feel peaceful?”
Feelings matter, but feelings are not infallible.
You can feel peaceful while making a terrible decision.
You can feel frightened while obeying God.
Jesus experienced anguish in Gethsemane while perfectly obeying His Father.
The biblical question is deeper:
Is it true?
Does it agree with God's revealed Word?
What does it say about Jesus?
Does it lead toward the Christ revealed in Scripture?
Does it produce obedience to Him?
Does it call sin what God calls sin?
Does it magnify grace without redefining repentance?
Does it honor the Gospel?
Does it survive examination?
Paul gives a remarkably similar command:
“Test everything; hold fast what is good.”
—1 Thessalonians 5:21
Notice the balance.
Christian discernment is neither gullibility nor cynicism.
The gullible Christian believes everything.
The cynical Christian believes nothing.
The discerning Christian tests everything and holds tightly to what is good.
There is a difference.
Discernment is not becoming the suspicious person in church who believes everyone except himself is deceived.
It is not watching sermons solely to catch mistakes.
It is not calling every theological disagreement demonic.
It is not declaring everyone outside your favorite denomination a false teacher.
It is not becoming spiritually paranoid.
And it certainly is not pretending that you personally possess an infallible ability to identify deception.
In fact, genuine discernment begins with enough humility to admit:
I can be deceived too.
That sentence is harder to say than it looks.
Because pride does something strange to discernment.
Eventually, a person can become so obsessed with identifying false teachers that he stops testing himself.
He detects pride everywhere...
except in the mirror.
He condemns manipulation...
while manipulating people.
He exposes harshness...
with cruelty.
He fights error...
without love.
And suddenly the person who wanted to defend truth has forgotten something John says only a few verses later:
“Beloved, let us love one another, for love is from God.”
Truth and love are not enemies.
The same apostle who commands Christians to test the spirits commands Christians to love one another.
So if your “discernment” makes you proud, cruel, unteachable, obsessed with accusation, or delighted by another person's downfall...
something has gone terribly wrong.
Biblical discernment should make you cling more tightly to Jesus, not become more impressed with yourself.
And perhaps the spirit most desperately needing examination today is not the one operating through somebody else's social-media feed.
Perhaps you need to examine what has been shaping you.
The voice saying:
“You don't need to forgive them.”
Test it.
The voice saying:
“Everybody does this. Your sin isn't serious.”
Test it.
The voice saying:
“You can follow Jesus without surrendering that part of your life.”
Test it.
The voice saying:
“You have sinned too badly. Jesus will never receive you again.”
Test that one too.
Because deception does not always tempt you toward arrogance.
Sometimes it drives you toward despair.
The enemy does not care whether he pushes you into self-righteousness or hopeless condemnation if either one keeps your eyes away from Christ.
One voice says:
“You don't need a Savior. You're good enough.”
Another says:
“You're too filthy for the Savior.”
The Gospel destroys both lies.
You are more sinful than your pride wants to admit.
And in Christ there is more grace than your shame dares to believe.
That is the scandal.
That is the grace.
At the cross, God does not pretend sin is insignificant.
Look at Jesus.
Nails.
Blood.
Mockery.
Darkness.
The innocent Son of God bearing what sinners deserved.
The cross tells you sin is so serious that redemption required the sacrifice of Christ.
But the cross simultaneously announces something breathtaking:
God loved sinners enough to give His Son.
Christ died for sins.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And the risen Jesus still receives repentant sinners.
Your darkest chapter does not have to become the title of your entire life.
Peter denied Jesus.
Thomas doubted.
Paul persecuted Christians.
The Corinthian church carried an embarrassing past.
The Gospel did not pretend their histories never happened.
Grace rewrote what those histories meant.
That is why Gospel Warrior keeps returning to this truth:
But understand what “Jesus rewrites everything” means.
It does not mean Jesus calls evil good.
It means Jesus takes guilty people, forgives them through His finished work, gives them new life, and begins transforming them by grace.
He does not merely improve the old story.
He makes sinners new.
And that means one of the most dangerous counterfeit spirits is any message that offers you transformation without Jesus.
Spirituality without Jesus.
Healing without Jesus.
Manifestation without Jesus.
Purpose without Jesus.
Prosperity without Jesus.
Self-discovery without Jesus.
Even “Christianity” without the biblical Jesus.
John will not permit it.
Jesus Christ stands in the middle of the test.
And notice something else.
John does not say believers should live terrified.
Immediately after warning them about deception, he writes:
—1 John 4:4
What a sentence.
Test every spirit...
but do not live afraid of every shadow.
Be discerning...
but not terrified.
Be watchful...
but remember Who lives in you.
The answer to deception is not obsession with darkness.
It is deeper allegiance to Christ.
Know Scripture so well that distortion becomes recognizable.
Know the Gospel so deeply that counterfeit gospels taste strange.
Know the character of Jesus revealed in Scripture so intimately that a distorted Christ cannot easily replace Him.
And when you fail?
Come back.
When you realize you believed something false?
Come back.
When pride fooled you?
Come back.
When you followed the wrong voice?
Come back.
When you defended something you now realize Scripture does not support?
Come back.
You do not have to defend yesterday's error simply because admitting you were wrong feels embarrassing.
Repentance is not humiliation before God.
It is liberation.
You can say:
“Lord, I was wrong.”
And grace will meet you there.
Maybe this article is exposing something uncomfortable.
Maybe you have been calling your desire “God's voice.”
Maybe you have been following personalities more carefully than Scripture.
Maybe someone has been controlling you through repeated claims that “God told me” while making you afraid to question them.
Maybe you have been consuming endless prophetic content while barely opening your Bible.
Maybe you have been so frightened of false teaching that suspicion has slowly replaced love.
Or maybe you have spent years believing the accusing voice saying God is finished with you.
Then hear this clearly:
Run to Jesus.
Not to hype.
Not to another personality.
Not to spiritual spectacle.
To Jesus.
Confess your sin.
Trust His mercy.
Return to His Word.
Ask God for wisdom.
Walk with mature believers who are willing to open Scripture with you.
Test what you hear.
Hold fast to what is good.
And above everything...
hold fast to Christ.
Not because every sentence I wrote should be treated as unquestionable.
Exactly the opposite.
Save it so you can return with your Bible open and test what you have read.
Send it privately to the believer who has been confused, wounded, manipulated, or afraid.

Sharing biblical truth can be one way we serve others and glorify God—but never confuse supporting a ministry with earning God's favor. If this ministry genuinely helps you know Christ, understand Scripture, and encourage others, then supporting the work is one practical way you may freely choose to help it reach more people.
Your support helps strengthen the work behind the articles, discipleship material, Gospel resources, and content being shared with believers and seekers.
“Test every spirit.”
Then remember the Person standing at the center of the test.
Jesus Christ.
Because the safest Christian is not the Christian who believes every supernatural claim.
And it is not the Christian who is terrified of everything supernatural.

It is the Christian whose eyes keep returning to Christ, whose Bible stays open, whose heart remains humble, whose sins are brought into the light, whose confidence rests in the Gospel, and whose deepest prayer remains:

“Jesus, whatever is false in me, expose it. Whatever is sinful in me, forgive it. Whatever is wounded in me, heal it. Whatever competes with You in me, tear it down. Teach me Your truth, and keep me close to You.”
Because one day every viral voice will become silent.
Every platform will disappear.
Every famous preacher will leave the stage.
Every algorithm will stop recommending.
Every human opinion will lose its applause.
But Jesus Christ will still be Lord.
So test the voices.
Test the teaching.
Test the claims.
Test even the things you desperately want to hear.
And when everything counterfeit has fallen away...
may the voice you refused to trade for all the others be the voice of the Shepherd who knew your name all along.
